knowledge_point.title: Finding a General Solution in Explicit Form

question.:question/problem: Find the general solution to the differential equation $y′=\frac{x^{2}}{y}.$ Assume $x+0>0.$ Take both sign branches on intervals where the radicand is positive and $y\ne 0.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
To find the general solution, we first separate the variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}y′ & =\frac{x^{2}}{y} \\ y\,\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x} & =x^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we integrate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int y\,\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}\,\mathrm{d}x & =\int x^{2}\,\mathrm{d}x \\ \int y\,\mathrm{d}y & =\int x^{2}\,\mathrm{d}x \\ \frac{y^{2}}{2} & =\frac{x^{3}}{3}+C\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the general solution to the differential equation (in implicit form) is

$$
\frac{y^{2}}{2}=\frac{x^{3}}{3}+C.
$$

We're required to write the solution in the form $y=y(x).$ By doing this, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}y^2 & =\frac{2 x^{3}}{3}+2C \\ y & =\pm\sqrt{\frac{2 x^{3}}{3}+2C} \\ y & =\pm\sqrt{\frac{2 x^{3}}{3}+K}\end{aligned}
$$

where $K=2C$ is an arbitrary real constant. Use either sign consistently on each interval where the radicand is positive.
